notes: Case stated appeal on hackney carriages used for pre-booked hire; statutory definitions under s.80 LG(MP)A 1976 are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Gladen: operator's licence not required for pre-booked hackney carriages
key_facts: Brentwood Borough Council prosecuted Mr Gladen five times for operating Ford Mondeos as private hire vehicles without a section 55 operator's licence.
On each occasion a customer telephoned '848 cars', a licensed hackney carriage was dispatched, and both vehicle and driver held valid hackney carriage licences.
The district judge acquitted on the basis that section 46(1)(d) did not apply where duly licensed hackney carriages and drivers were used.
The council appealed by way of case stated; Collins and Silber JJ heard the appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by way of case stated against acquittals in magistrates' court for offences under section 46(1)(d) of the 1976 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; an operator's licence under section 55 is not required to dispatch licensed hackney carriages for pre-booked private hire; defendant's costs ordered from central funds.
enrichment.ratio: Section 46(1)(d) must be read with the technical definitions in section 80: 'operate' means making provision for bookings of a private hire vehicle, which excludes hackney carriages; requiring an operator's licence for licensed hackney carriages would make section 46(1)(e) absurd.
legal_issues: Whether section 46(1)(d) requires an operator's licence when licensed hackney carriages are used for telephone bookings
Whether 'operate any vehicle as a private hire vehicle' includes hackney carriages
Whether section 67 authorises what section 46(1)(d) would otherwise prohibit

notes: Confiscation realisable-assets stage and matrimonial home; Benjafield/Rezvi distinction is carefully applied.

enrichment.short_title: Ahmed and Qureshi: no discretion on realisable assets at confiscation
key_facts: Ahmed and Qureshi were convicted of money laundering conspiracies and received large benefit findings but confiscation orders based on realisable assets.
The Crown Court included each appellant's half share in the matrimonial home, which the families said would probably have to be sold.
The judge accepted he had discretion but found no exceptional circumstances to exclude the home; the appeals challenged that exercise.
Benefit findings were not appealed; the issue was solely assessment of realisable property under section 74.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) appeals against confiscation orders made after conviction for money laundering conspiracies.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; the court has no discretion at the realisable-assets stage to exclude the matrimonial home; Article 8 may be engaged only at enforcement if sale is sought.
enrichment.ratio: After the 1995 amendments the court must make a confiscation order equal to benefit or realisable assets, whichever is less; 'the amount appearing to the court' in section 71(6)(b) refers to valuation not discretion; Rezvi injustice discretion applies to benefit assumptions, not the arithmetic of realisable property.
legal_issues: Whether the court retains discretion to exclude matrimonial home value when assessing realisable assets
Whether Article 8 requires reading discretion into section 71(6)(b)
When third-party and family Article 8 rights arise in confiscation proceedings

notes: Dual Bhutan asylum appeals on statelessness burden and IAT reasoning; split outcomes are clearly explained.

enrichment.short_title: Darji and Gurung: Bhutanese statelessness and asylum appeals
key_facts: Two ethnic Nepalese asylum seekers from Bhutan raised statelessness as barring lawful return.
The IAT in Darji reversed the burden of proof and found statelessness without adequate evidence of Bhutanese nationality law application.
In Gurung the adjudicator found a well-founded fear of persecution on orthodox grounds, but the IAT sidetracked into citizenship and gave no proper reasons for overturning that finding.
Country evidence showed precarious status for southern Nepalese but a maintained citizenship register.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal permission appeals on substantive asylum and removal challenges after Immigration Appeal Tribunal decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Home Secretary's appeal allowed in Darji; Gurung's appeal allowed and the adjudicator's persecution finding restored; Darji's statelessness finding overturned.
enrichment.ratio: The burden rests on the claimant to prove statelessness on reasonable likelihood; non-registration in Bhutan's register does not prove statelessness; persecution findings cannot rest solely on a statelessness premise; an IAT must give adequate reasons when oversetting an adjudicator on merits.
legal_issues: Burden and standard of proof for statelessness in asylum cases
Effect of Bhutanese nationality laws of 1958 and 1985
Whether risk findings survive rejection of statelessness
Adequacy of IAT reasons on persecution grounds
linked_authorities: Revenko v Home Secretary [2000] Imm AR 610

notes: AG reference on serial armed robberies; double jeopardy adjustment and guideline authorities are clearly applied.

enrichment.short_title: AG Ref 52/2004: unduly lenient armed robbery series
key_facts: A 21-year-old pleaded guilty to six offences including four robberies of vulnerable occupied premises at night using masks, crowbars, axes, knives and a hammer.
The Crown Court imposed concurrent sentences totalling five years' imprisonment.
Victims were terrified; substantial cash and property were taken; the offender had 121 previous convictions and a history of custody.
The Attorney General referred the sentences as unduly lenient under section 36.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the 1988 Act against concurrent Crown Court sentences for robbery and related offences.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; robbery sentences quashed and replaced with seven years concurrent each, giving a total of seven years after double jeopardy; ancillary sentences unchanged.
enrichment.ratio: Serial planned robberies of occupied vulnerable premises at night with weapons and masks required a significantly higher sentence than five years; an expected starting point was eight or nine years, reduced to seven for double jeopardy.
legal_issues: Whether five years was unduly lenient for a series of armed robberies
Application of double jeopardy on an Attorney General's reference
Proper concurrent structure for multiple robbery counts

notes: Standards Board appeal on councillor interests and suspension; breach findings upheld but sanction reduced.

enrichment.short_title: Murphy: councillor code breach upheld, suspension reduced
key_facts: Cllr Murphy was criticised by the Local Government Ombudsman for participating in a planning committee decision despite a declared alternative development proposal.
He remained at a council meeting discussing the Ombudsman's report, spoke on it, and abstained from voting despite advice to withdraw.
A Standards Board case tribunal found breaches of personal and prejudicial interest rules and suspended him for one year.
He received conflicting advice from officers, including that section 31A(5) permitted speaking but not voting.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal under section 79(15) against Standards Board case tribunal findings and one-year suspension.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal against breach findings dismissed; appeal against one-year suspension allowed and substituted with four months' suspension.
enrichment.ratio: A councillor exclusively named and criticised in an Ombudsman report has a personal and prejudicial interest requiring withdrawal from discussion; 'well-being' in the model code is broad; but where the interest was public knowledge and advice was confusing, a one-year suspension was disproportionate.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'well-being' in the members' code of conduct
Whether being named in an Ombudsman report creates a prejudicial interest
Compatibility with Articles 6, 8 and 10 ECHR
Proportionality of suspension sanction

notes: Whiplash eggshell-skull damages appeal; court reassessed general and earnings losses without remittal.

enrichment.short_title: Mullins v Gray: eggshell skull whiplash damages increased
key_facts: Mrs Mullins suffered a whiplash injury when the defendant drove into her stationary car at traffic lights in March 1999.
Liability was admitted; the judge awarded £12,900 globally including £6,000 general damages and six months' loss of earnings.
She had a pre-existing anxious disposition that heightened pain perception but no recognised psychiatric disorder.
Medical evidence linked continuing pain to the whiplash injury; the judge was deflected by psychiatric evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal civil appeal against county court assessment of damages for whiplash injury.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; general damages set at £20,000, past loss of earnings about £34,000, future loss £13,000; indemnity costs from 21 days before trial; leave to House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: The tortfeasor takes the victim as found; heightened pain from an anxious disposition does not require medical proof of a psychiatric disorder when the claim is for physical pain caused by the accident; psychiatric-evidence requirements apply only to psychiatric injury claims.
legal_issues: Whether medical evidence is required to establish eggshell-skull susceptibility to pain
Proper assessment of general damages for prolonged whiplash symptoms
Whether loss of earnings should extend beyond six months given psychiatric overlay
Whether remittal was required for reassessment

notes: AG reference on aggravated burglary and witness bribery; consecutive sentence structure corrected.

enrichment.short_title: AG Ref 92/2004: aggravated burglary and witness bribery sentences
key_facts: The offender broke into a couple's home at night, threatened the male victim with a kitchen knife and a bed slat with a nail, and stole cash and property.
While awaiting trial he participated in a plan to bribe the victim with up to £5,000 to retract evidence; co-conspirators received shorter sentences.
He pleaded guilty to aggravated burglary and conspiracy to pervert the course of justice and received six and two years concurrently.
He was on licence from a previous sentence and had significant but non-violent antecedents.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 against concurrent sentences for aggravated burglary and conspiracy to pervert the course of justice.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; total sentence increased to seven and a half years comprising six years for burglary and eighteen months consecutive for perverting the course of justice, with double jeopardy accounted for.
enrichment.ratio: Aggravated burglary of sleeping occupants at night with weapons and a subsequent bribery attempt while on licence required a substantially higher total sentence; the conspiracy sentence should have run consecutively, not concurrently, to the burglary term.
legal_issues: Whether six years concurrent was unduly lenient for aggravated burglary plus bribery
Whether conspiracy to pervert the course of justice should be consecutive
Effect of unexpired licence period on resentencing

notes: Prison medical correspondence Article 8 appeal; proportionality analysis reverses Collins J.

enrichment.short_title: Szuluk: prison reading of medical correspondence lawful
key_facts: A Category B prisoner with a life-threatening brain condition sought confidential correspondence with his NHS neuroradiologist.
The governor initially permitted confidential mail but was overruled; correspondence was opened and checked by the prison medical officer under PSO 1000 Ch.36.
Collins J held the restriction disproportionate; the governor and Home Secretary appealed.
The claimant was later allowed confidential correspondence at another prison pending appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal against judicial review quashing prison restrictions on outside medical correspondence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; reading medical correspondence by the prison medical officer was a proportionate Article 8(2) interference in this high-security context.
enrichment.ratio: Prison Rule 34 and PSO 1000 permit flexible but security-based restrictions; governors may grant confidentiality where satisfied security is not jeopardised but are not obliged to; reading by a medically qualified officer is the least invasive effective measure and does not deny the essence of Article 8 rights.
legal_issues: Whether Article 8 requires confidential prisoner correspondence with an outside medical specialist
Proportionality of PSO 1000 Ch.36.21 monitoring for Category A unit prisoners
Whether life-threatening illness makes refusal to waive monitoring unlawful
Proper margin of appreciation or legality review of prison policy

notes: Second homelessness application under Fahia; identical-facts comparison and Southwark errors noted.

enrichment.short_title: Griffin v Southwark: repeat homelessness application rejected
key_facts: Ms Griffin and her partner made a joint 2002 homelessness application; Southwark accepted a full duty but she refused an Aylesbury Estate offer.
After discharge of duty and loss of temporary accommodation she made a fresh 2004 application alone.
Southwark refused to consider the 2004 application as based on the same facts; its letters inconsistently referred to review rights.
By December 2002 she had separated from her partner, the only asserted difference at the time of the 2004 application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review to quash refusal to consider a fresh section 184 homelessness application.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the 2004 application was based on the same facts as the determined 2002 application so Southwark was not obliged to reopen inquiries.
enrichment.ratio: Following R v Harrow ex parte Fahia, a local authority must consider a further homelessness application unless it is based on exactly the same facts; separation from her partner had already occurred before the 2002 offer and final refusal, so no new material difference existed.
legal_issues: Whether Fahia or Campisi governs repeat homelessness applications
What constitutes 'exactly the same facts' for a second section 184 application
Whether applying alone after prior joint application is a material change
Effect of Southwark's procedural errors on the substantive decision

notes: Planning appeal quashed for PPG3 sequential-test illogic and inadequate affordable-housing reasons.

enrichment.short_title: Oxford City Council v SoS: Leafield Road planning appeal quashed

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning Appeals (Determination by Inspectors) (Inquiries Procedure) (England) Rules 2000

key_facts: Oxford City Council refused planning permission for 38 dwellings on Leafield Road, Cowley; a 2002 inspector dismissed Pye's appeal.
Pye reapplied with increased affordable housing; a 2004 inspector allowed the appeal.
The site was vacant urban land but not previously developed land under PPG 3 Annex C.
The Secretary of State conceded inadequate reasons and did not defend the 2004 decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court section 288 challenge to a planning inspector's decision allowing a second residential development appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Council's challenge succeeded; the 2004 appeal decision quashed for irrational PPG 3 sequential-test reasoning and failure to resolve affordable shared-ownership housing, with inadequate reasons under regulation 19.
enrichment.ratio: It is illogical to hold that because a greenfield site fits none of paragraph 30's priority classifications it cannot conflict with PPG 3's search sequence; an inspector must give clear reasons for departing from an earlier appeal decision and must determine whether proposed shared ownership housing meets Circular 6/98 affordability.
legal_issues: Proper application of PPG 3 paragraph 30 sequential test to non-PDL urban land
Whether departure from a previous inspector's decision was adequately reasoned
Definition of affordable housing under Circular 6/98 for shared ownership
Regulation 19 adequacy of reasons and substantial prejudice
